notes.504.14: Finns (Finnar) are the Sami. First stanza, in prose order: the generous prince himself found most clearly how the mighty spells of the sorcerous Finns saved the very great Thorir, when the fire-sender of the mast-heads struck the Hound across the shoulders with the gold-adorned sword; smooth, it would hardly bite. 'Fire-sender of the mast-heads' is evidently a kenning for Olaf as a generous lord; its exact construal is uncertain. Second stanza, roughly: the fir of gold [a man] who taunts Thorir denies true valour; I know this from home: who would see greater deeds than the great-hearted Hound's, when the might of the storm of cross-fences [battle; its might, a warrior, i.e. Thorir], he who pressed forward, dared to strike against the king's man? 'Cross-fences' are probably shields, and 'battle-hall' (Gunnrann) is a shield too, part of the same kenning; 'kononɢ manni' is 'the king's man', King Olaf. The construal of this half-stanza is uncertain.
notes.9.15: The transcription doubles many words ('ŭptaca uppta-ka', 'ackerin atkeriɴ Atkeriɴ', 'draga draga', 'fiolkyngi fiolkingi'), apparently variant spellings set side by side; each is translated once. Line 9.28 repeats the place name of 9.27 in the same way. The bracket in 9.16 is an editor's remark on a letter form, not text. 'ſiþir' (9.27) is taken as síðir, 'at last'. Finns are the Sami.
notes.157.h: Finns are the Sami. The numbers 'í(?+)j' and 'xí(?+)j' are read as ii and xii; the edition marks them as doubtful. Landed men (lendir menn) are chieftains holding land from the king.
notes.435.9: Olafshellir means 'Olaf's Cave'. The edition's (+K) marks letters supplied from another copy; they are translated as given. 'ſt(+K)' (435.17) is read as sætr, 'shieling'. A letter of the name Græningar (435.21) is marked uncertain.

then in the evening he came to the ships. The
Finns made in the night a furious storm
by sorcery
and a tempest at sea;
but the king had [them] take up
the anchors and
hoist sail, and they beat [to windward] through the night
along the land; then again, as
often before, the king's good fortune was stronger than
the sorcery of the Finns. They managed to beat [their way]
through the night, at last, off the coast of Balagard
the coast of Balagard
packs, no worse than on level ground.
Then the king went back down to where
his quarters were, [the place] now called Olafshellir. A spring
is also there near the cave, and the king washed
himself in it; and if people's livestock fall sick
in the valley and drink of that water,
then they recover from the sickness. Then the king went to
his meal, and all of them; and when the king was
fed, he asked whether there was any shieling
in the valley, up from the scree and
near the mountain, where they might lodge for
the night. And Brusi says there are shielings called
Græningar, and no one can stay there
at night because of the walking of trolls and
evil beings that are there by the shieling.
Then the king said that they should make ready for their journey,
and says that he wanted to be there for the night
Chapter 204. Of the Landed Men.
Now it shall be told what they were
doing in Norway during these times. Thorir
Hund had made the journey to the Finns these two
winters, and both winters he had been long in the mountains and had got
a vast amount of wealth. He had many kinds of trade with the Finns.
He had twelve reindeer coats made for himself there
with such great sorcery that
no weapon took hold on them, and much less than
on a ring-mail coat. And the following spring
Thorir fitted out a longship that he owned and manned it
with his housecarls. He called together the farmers
son of Arnfinn Armodsson, brother's son of Arni
Armodsson. On the other side of Kalf
Arnason, Thorir Hund went forward. Olaf
the king struck at Thorir Hund across the shoulders;
the sword did not bite, and it looked as if
dust flew up from the reindeer coat.
Sigvat speaks of this:
The generous one found most clearly how the spells,
the prince himself, the mighty-strong [spells]
of the sorcery-wise Finns
saved the very great Thorir,
when the fire-sender, on the Hound,
of the mast-heads, with the gold-adorned
(smooth, it would least of all bite) sword struck across the shoulders.
Thorir struck at the king, and they then exchanged a few
blows, and the king's sword did not bite
where the reindeer coat was in front, but still
Thorir was wounded in the hand. And Sigvat said:
The fir-tree denies true valour
of gold (and this I know from home),
who would see greater deeds than the Hound's,
the great-hearted one's, [the fir] who taunts Thorir,
when [he], of the cross-fences, dared,
the might that pressed forward,
of the storm, to strike against
of the battle-hall [shield], the king's man.
The king said to Bjorn the Marshal: Beat
the dog whom iron does not bite. Bjorn
turned the axe in his hand and struck with
the hammer; the blow landed on Thorir's shoulder, and
it was a very heavy blow, and Thorir reeled at it
